deep.topic: This session takes Week 2's function material conceptually rather than computationally, starting from what a function actually is: a rule assigning to every element of a domain A exactly one element of a codomain B, and what breaks if either the totality clause or the uniqueness clause is dropped. It works through why the vertical line test detects a failure of uniqueness of output while the horizontal line test detects a failure of uniqueness of input, and why a graph can pass one and fail the other. It separates the injective condition (no element of the codomain is hit twice) from the surjective condition (no element is missed), distinguishes range from codomain, and establishes why only a bijection can be inverted - a collision makes the inverse ambiguous, a gap makes it undefined. It examines why the logarithm carries the restrictions b > 0, b != 1 and x > 0, and why exponential and logarithmic functions swap domain and range as inverses of each other. It covers why a piecewise function's conditions must be disjoint (a boundary point assigned twice with different values would break single-valuedness) while the branches are under no obligation to agree there. It closes on why the degree and leading coefficient alone govern a polynomial's behaviour far from the origin, because every lower-degree term becomes negligible relative to the leading term.

fast.topic: The Monday fast hour covers Week 2 of Nigerian Peoples and Culture, Dr Abimbola Oyarinu's lecture on intergroup relations among pre-colonial Nigerian peoples. It opens with the definition of inter-group relations as interaction between two or more distinct linguistic and cultural groups, the two identifiers of a group (culture and language), and the scale of Nigerian diversity - over 348 language groups and 374 ethnic groups. The bulk of the hour works through the four indicators used to reconstruct pre-colonial interaction. Traditions of origin covers the shared Kanuri and Hausa myths tracing to Baghdad through Saif and Bayajidda, Bayajidda settling among the Kanuri and marrying the Mai's daughter, the Kisra legend founding the Yoruba and Borgu kingdoms with the Ooni of Ife as Kisra's brother, the Yoruba-Benin link through Oranmiyan and Eweka, and the Umu-Ezechinma Igbo and Isoko ties to Edo. Conflict covers the Oyo-Nupe wars and the Bariba-Yoruba alliance, the Kano-Katsina wars over trade routes, Jukun conquest over the Kanuri, Hausa, Igala, Idoma and Ebira, Benin's expansion to Auchi, Idah, Itsekiri, Urhobo, Isoko, Okpe and Eko (Lagos) with the Benin-descended Lagos kings Ado and Asipa, and the Igala-Nsukka Igbo wars that left the Illah speaking Igbo while their masquerades speak Igala. Trade and commerce covers the Jukun salt-for-Tiv-firewood exchange, Kanem-Bornu's role in the trans-Saharan trade as the channel for Yoruba and Nupe participation, Ibibio land as the corridor between hinterland Igbo and coastal Efik and Ijaw, and Nupe goods traded to the Yoruba. Religion covers shared indigenous practices and borrowed deities and cults: Yoruba Igunu from Nupe Ndakogbaya, Ibibio-origin Ibini Ukpabi among the Igbo, Efik-origin Ekpe and Ekpo among Igbo subgroups, and the Bori cult across Hausaland. The hour closes with Nigeria's six geo-political zones and their dominant ethnic groups, and Nigeria's history dating back to 39,000 BC.

deep.topic: The Tuesday deep hour takes the week-2 electrostatics material conceptually rather than numerically. It works through what Coulomb's law actually claims - force proportional to the product of charge magnitudes and to the inverse square of separation, acting along the line joining them - and where the law stops being valid, namely point charges at rest with spheres treated from their centres. It then examines the superposition principle as an experimental fact rather than a definition: that the pairwise force between two charges is unaffected by a third charge, which is precisely what licenses applying a two-body law to a many-body system. The session covers what the electric field is as a quantity, why it is defined as force per unit vanishingly small test charge, and why it belongs to the source charges rather than to the test charge that reveals it. Field lines are read as a representation: what their direction, spacing and non-crossing encode, and why a single isolated charge produces a field but feels no net force from its own field. The session then contrasts the vector nature of the electric field with the scalar nature of electric potential, and draws out the consequence that fields can cancel where potentials add and potentials can cancel where fields add. It closes on the structure of the Lorentz force - which term requires motion, which term does work and which cannot.

fast.topic: The Tuesday fast hour covers Week 2 of Introduction to Web Technologies, which is a protocol-and-markup survey rather than a coding week. It opens with the four transfer protocols the week is titled after - HTTP as the insecure foundation of web data communication, HTTPS as its encrypted counterpart, FTP as the unencrypted file transfer protocol, and SFTP as the secure extension that adds encryption and strong authentication. It then moves to markup languages as the backbone of structured content: HTML for structuring web content through elements, tags and attributes; XML for storing and exchanging structured data using user-defined tags; SVG for scalable two-dimensional vector graphics; MathML for mathematical notation; and XHTML as HTML reformulated as an XML application. The email block follows, splitting SMTP (sending and relaying outgoing mail, with its HELO, MAIL FROM and RCPT TO commands) from the retrieval protocols POP3 (downloads for offline access) and IMAP (keeps mail on the server and synchronises across devices), plus MIME for non-ASCII text and attachments. Next comes the Domain Name System: domain name resolution, name-to-IP mapping and reverse lookup, the root domain, TLD, second-level domain and subdomain hierarchy, resolvers and authoritative servers, MX records, and DNSSEC for signing DNS data against cache poisoning. The hour closes on web communication protocols - WebSocket's full-duplex persistent TCP connection, REST's stateless resource-based use of GET, POST, PUT and DELETE mapped to CRUD, and SOAP's strict XML messaging - with their stated advantages and disadvantages. The emphasis throughout is memorising acronym expansions and being able to discriminate each pair, since that is what the assessment format rewards.

deep.topic: The Wednesday deep hour takes Week 2's material conceptually, without traces or arithmetic. It starts from the lesson's own definition of a problem-solving strategy - a plan, made of multiple steps, used to find a solution or overcome a challenge - and the claim that different problems require different strategies, so that choosing and then studying a strategy's rules and procedures is part of solving rather than a delay. It then works through the internal mechanism of each of the six named strategies: brainstorming's dependence on volume of ideas and on deferred criticism; the heuristic trade of rationality for speed, valid only where a sub-optimal solution is acceptable; trial-and-error's cost scaling with the number of candidate solutions; means-ends analysis fixing the intended solution in advance and decomposing the problem so each part gets its best-suited approach; abstraction deleting the attributes that will not help reach a solution and leaving a model; and analogy transferring understanding from a known system, valid only while the underlying principles are the same. For each, the session asks what it costs and under what conditions it fails. The second half covers the conceptual basis of the week's classifications: well-defined versus ill-defined, and routine versus non-routine as a question of whether a standard method exists rather than whether arithmetic is involved. It closes on solvability - what the universal Turing machine contributes to the idea of an algorithm, and why "unsolvable" is a claim about the absence of a systematic decision procedure for every input rather than a claim that no answer exists, with decidable and undecidable problems and the halting problem treated in those terms.

fast.topic: The Wednesday fast hour covers GST_122 Week 2, "Communication and Meaning", whose organising claim is that the ultimate goal of communication is that meaning is conveyed accurately, and that communication is not solely about words. Start with semiotics - the field of signs and symbols and the role they play in everyday interaction - and the point that meaning travels through non-verbal signs as well as language. Then drill the central distinction the course examines on: denotative meaning (the literal, dictionary sense) versus connotative meaning (the implied or suggested sense, carrying cultural and emotional associations), practising on example words rather than reciting the definitions. Next take the two named sources of confusion, hazardous homophones and ambiguity, and learn the discriminating test between them: written down, a homophone problem disappears while an ambiguous sentence is still readable two ways. Work through the week's case study, "The Ambiguity Challenge in Project Coordination", in which a single ambiguous task-assignment sentence produced conflicting interpretations of tasks and responsibilities across a project team. Close by memorising the lesson's definition of effective communication - conveying intended meanings accurately while being mindful of the broader cultural and emotional associations of words - and the six named competencies: Semiotic Awareness, Contextual Interpretation, Clarity in Expression, Active Listening, Conflict Resolution and Cultural Sensitivity. Since the course tests classification of examples, spend the last ten minutes labelling sample sentences as denotative, connotative, homophone or ambiguity.

deep.topic: This session works the same Week 2 function material as problems: reading a question, choosing a method, executing it accurately and checking the result. It covers evaluating compositions in the correct order and seeing that f o g and g o f differ; finding the largest domain of an expression that combines a logarithm with a denominator, where two separate restrictions must both be imposed; completing the square on a quadratic to locate its vertex, axis of symmetry and direction of opening; solving an absolute-value equation by splitting it into its two cases; solving an exponential equation by isolating the power and recognising it as a power of the base; evaluating a piecewise function at and either side of its boundary point by first deciding which condition the input satisfies; recovering a line's equation from two points via the slope formula and point-slope form; and solving a logarithmic equation by combining logs, clearing the log, and then rejecting the root that violates the domain. The written questions are diagnostic: naming exactly where standard wrong routes go astray - squaring an absolute-value equation and manufacturing extraneous roots, treating 5^x as 5 times x, taking c to be the vertex y-coordinate - and checking a vertex by independent means before reading end behaviour off a cubic.

fast.topic: The Thursday fast hour covers Week 2 of General Physics Practical II: Ohmic resistance and the experiment to verify Ohm's law. Start with the statement of Ohm's law - current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it at constant temperature - and the equation V = IR with each symbol and unit defined, plus the distinction between ohmic resistors (constant R, straight V-I line through the origin, reversible behaviour) and non-ohmic ones such as varistors, photoresistors and thermistors. Then drill the two combination rules: series resistors carry the same current and add as R = R1 + R2 + ... + RN, while parallel resistors share the same potential difference and combine as 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ..., checked against the worked values 10 ohm, 20 ohm and 30 ohm giving 60 ohm in series and 5.45 ohm in parallel. Next walk the Praxilabs virtual Ohmic Resistor procedure in order: wire the breadboard circuit, connect the voltmeter in parallel and the ammeter in series, connect the DC power supply, set R1 between 1 and 20 kilohm, apply a chosen voltage with the knob or slider, press Record, and repeat six more times for seven data points before the Excel file downloads. Finish on the analysis that carries the marks: plot V on the y-axis against I in mA on the x-axis, map V = IR onto y = mx + c so that the gradient is the resistance and a zero intercept confirms no systematic offset, watch the unit trap that volts per milliamp gives kilohms, and compute the percentage error against the 1 kilohm default value, which must fall within 5 per cent for the verification to pass.

deep.topic: The Friday deep hour works the same week-2 material as problems. It concentrates on setting up superposition calculations from a free-body sketch: identifying each pairwise force, deciding from the signs whether it is an attraction or a repulsion, and therefore whether contributions add or subtract along the line - the single step where most marks are lost. It carries the arithmetic through with unit conversions (nm, um, nC, uC) intact and with the Coulomb constant applied correctly. The session works the three problems set in the deck: the electron on the line between two protons 3.6 nm apart, the three collinear charges of -18 uC, -12 uC and +24 uC and the net force on each, and the +2.00 nC / -5.00 nC pair whose resultant field at an intermediate point must be found and then converted to a force on an electron placed there. It also drills route selection - recognising when symmetry gives an answer instantly versus when a brute-force component sum is unavoidable - and error diagnosis, such as spotting that a net force larger than either contributing force means opposing contributions were wrongly added. Finally it covers checking a finished answer, either by dimensional analysis or by recomputing through a second independent relation. The emphasis throughout is on the set-up and the check, not on recalling statements.

fast.topic: Week 2 review: re-work every check question you got wrong Mon-Thu, then cold, on paper, do one composite evaluated in both orders, one vertex by completing the square checked against -b/(2a), and one three-charge collinear superposition where you settle every direction from a sketch before touching the arithmetic. Then state, without notes, why potentials add as signed numbers while fields add as vectors. Finish by settling which two topics Sunday gets from the four scores so far.

deep.topic: The Saturday session is COS_102 applied, working the week's method through on concrete cases rather than restating it. The student is given stated problems and has to classify them by testing rather than by surface appearance - recognising that Bridget's 50-question exam-marks problem is non-routine despite using only arithmetic, that the parking-space area is routine because a known formula applies, and that "approximate the number of hairs on your head" is non-routine rather than unsolvable. Scenarios are then read and matched to the strategy actually in use, including cases designed to mislead: XYZ Corporation's $2bn turnover target decomposed into quarterly and regional targets is means-ends analysis, while the doctor converging several weaker rays on a deep tumour after recalling an army dividing to take a fortress is analogy, not means-ends, despite the division into smaller parts. The session runs the two ordered procedures of the week in sequence - the three analogy steps and the three steps for attacking a non-routine problem. It traces the substitution puzzle one replacement at a time, obtaining BOOOB from BOB via the rules OB->BOOB and BOB->O. Finally it diagnoses attempts that went wrong: a heuristic applied to a routine problem where an exact answer is required, a brainstorming session ruined by immediate criticism, and a premature conclusion that a substitution puzzle does not come out. The halting problem is met applied, as a request to write a program that decides termination for any input.

fast.topic: Catch-up: sit the Week 1 question sets, now seven days old and due - all seven of them, since this is the first retest of the semester and the retention gap is the whole point. Then clear anything left over from this week: the CSC_106 protocol and markup acronyms and the GST_112 four indicators of intergroup relations with their named examples are the two that most reward a second pass, both being pure recall that is cheapest to bank now. If time remains, re-read the PHY_108 series and parallel combination rules.

questions.q: The definition of a function f: A → B says every element of A is assigned **exactly one** element of B. If "exactly one" were weakened to "at least one", what specifically breaks?
options: The domain would no longer be the whole of A.
The symbol f(x) would no longer name a definite value.
The range could become larger than the codomain.
The function could no longer be surjective.
questions.concept: The uniqueness clause in the definition of a function
questions.why: Weakening 'exactly one' to 'at least one' lets a single input carry two outputs, so the notation f(x) no longer denotes a single definite value.

questions.q: The vertical line test detects the failure of which clause?
options: That the domain is an unbroken interval.
That every element of the codomain is used.
That no two inputs share an output.
That each input has only one output.
questions.concept: What the vertical line test actually tests
questions.why: A vertical line collects every point with the same first coordinate, so two intersections mean one input has two outputs - a failure of uniqueness of output, not of injectivity or surjectivity.

questions.q: A map f: A → B is described as surjective but not injective. Which must be true?
options: Every element of B is reached, and some element of B twice.
Every element of A is reached, and some element of A twice.
The range is a proper subset of the codomain of f.
f has a well-defined inverse on the whole of B.
questions.concept: Distinguishing surjective from injective
questions.why: Surjective means every element of the codomain is reached; not injective means some element of the codomain is reached by more than one input.

questions.q: f: A → B is surjective but fails to be injective. What exactly goes wrong when you try to define f⁻¹?
options: f⁻¹ would have a domain larger than B.
f⁻¹ would be undefined at some elements of B.
Some element of B would have to be sent to two different elements of A.
f⁻¹ ∘ f would be the identity on B instead of on A.
questions.concept: Why invertibility requires injectivity
questions.why: If two inputs share an output, the proposed inverse would have to send that one output to two different inputs, which is not a function.

questions.q: log_b(x) is defined only for b > 0 **and b ≠ 1**. What is the reason for excluding b = 1?
options: A power of the number 1 has no defined value at all.
log₁(x) would come out negative whenever x is below 1.
The curve y = 1^x would fail to cross the y-axis anywhere.
Every power of 1 equals 1, so nothing else is reachable.
questions.concept: Why the logarithm base excludes b = 1
questions.why: Since 1^y = 1 for every y, the function 1^x is constant and hits no other value, so it has no inverse to serve as log base 1.

questions.q: In f(x) = 2x + 1 for x ≤ 0 and f(x) = x² − 3 for x > 0, why is the second condition written x > 0 rather than x ≥ 0?
options: Because x = 0 is already assigned by the first branch.
Because the expression x² − 3 has no defined value when x is 0.
Because the two branches are required to agree in value at x = 0.
Because the graph of a function must be unbroken at a boundary.
questions.concept: Why piecewise conditions must be disjoint
questions.why: x = 0 is already covered by x <= 0; using x >= 0 in the second branch would assign x = 0 both 1 and -3, destroying single-valuedness.

questions.q: Why is |x| defined by two cases (x if x ≥ 0, −x if x < 0) instead of the instruction "remove the minus sign"?
options: Because −x is a positive number whatever the value of x.
Because the graph of |x| has to be smooth at the origin.
Because which case applies depends on x, not on a visible sign.
Because absolute value is defined for real inputs only.
questions.concept: Why absolute value is defined by cases
questions.why: The rule cannot be 'remove the minus sign' because in |x - 3| there is no visible sign - which case applies is determined by the value of x.

questions.q: For a polynomial of degree n with leading coefficient aₙ, why do those two numbers alone decide the shape of the graph far from the origin?
options: Because the lower-degree terms become zero once |x| is large.
Because every other term, divided by aₙxⁿ, tends to 0 as |x| grows.
Because polynomials of equal degree have identical graphs.
Because a₀ is only the y-intercept and never affects shape.
questions.concept: Why degree and leading coefficient fix end behaviour
questions.why: Dividing any lower-degree term by the leading term gives a ratio tending to 0 as |x| grows, so the leading term dominates - the other terms become negligible relative to it, not zero in themselves.

questions.q: Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function. Explain the difference using the slide's set language — "A has many B" versus "B can have many A" — and say which of those two situations is allowed.
questions.concept: Every function is a relation; the converse fails on the uniqueness clause
questions.why: A relation is any pairing of elements of A with elements of B. A function is a relation with one extra restriction: each element of A is paired with exactly one element of B. In the slide's language, 'B can have many A' is allowed - several different inputs may share one output, which is just a many-to-one function. What is forbidden is 'A has many B': one input carrying several outputs. That is the situation the vertical line test detects, and it is precisely what stops a relation from being a function.

questions.q: The vertical line test and the horizontal line test look almost identical but answer different questions. Explain what property each one is testing and why a graph can pass one and fail the other.
questions.concept: The two line tests check different clauses of the pairing
questions.why: The vertical line test checks whether each input has only one output - that is, whether the relation is a function at all. The horizontal line test checks whether each output comes from only one input - that is, whether the function is injective and therefore invertible. A graph can pass the first and fail the second: y = x^2 is a perfectly good function, since every x gives exactly one y, but the line y = 4 meets it twice, so two inputs share an output and it has no inverse on R. The two tests scan in perpendicular directions because they interrogate opposite halves of the pairing.

questions.q: Explain why f(x) = b^x and g(x) = log_b(x) are called inverses, and why the domain of one is the range of the other. Use this to explain why log_b(x) is undefined for x ≤ 0.
questions.concept: Exponential and logarithm as mutual inverses, with domain and range exchanged
questions.why: log_b(x) is defined as the exponent to which b must be raised to give x, so b^(log_b x) = x and log_b(b^x) = x - each undoes the other, which is exactly what makes them inverses. Under inversion the domain and range swap: b^x has domain all reals and range (0, inf), so log_b(x) has domain (0, inf) and range all reals. That is why log_b(x) is undefined for x <= 0 - no real exponent applied to a positive base ever produces zero or a negative number, so there is nothing for the logarithm to return.

questions.q: A slide states that in f(x) = ax² + bx + c, "c is the y-coordinate of the vertex". Explain why this is false as written, what c genuinely is, and the one special case in which the slide's claim happens to be true.
questions.concept: What c actually is in ax^2 + bx + c, and the single case where the slide is accidentally right
questions.why: c is the y-intercept: setting x = 0 gives f(0) = c, so c is the height at which the curve crosses the y-axis. The vertex sits at x = -b/(2a), and its y-coordinate is f(-b/(2a)) = c - b^2/(4a), which differs from c by b^2/(4a). The slide's claim is therefore false whenever b is not zero. The one special case in which it happens to be true is b = 0: the vertex then lies on the y-axis at x = 0, so the vertex's y-coordinate and the y-intercept are the same point, and both equal c.

questions.q: Charges q₁ and q₂ sit 1 m apart. A third charge q₃ is then brought into the region. What happens to the force that q₂ exerts on q₁?
options: It grows, because there is now more total charge nearby.
It is unchanged; q₃ contributes a separate force that is added vectorially.
It falls, because q₃ screens off part of q₁'s field.
It changes only if q₃ lies on the line joining q₁ and q₂.
questions.concept: Superposition: pairwise forces are independent of the other charges present
questions.why: Bringing q3 in adds a third force vectorially but leaves the q1-q2 force exactly as Coulomb's law gives it - charge does not pool and there is no electrostatic screening in vacuum.

questions.q: The electric field is defined as **E** = **F**/q₀ using a test charge q₀ that is taken to be vanishingly small. Why must q₀ be small?
options: A large q₀ would disturb the source charges and change the field being measured.
The definition is only valid for charges of magnitude smaller than one coulomb.
F grows in proportion to q₀², so the ratio F/q₀ is constant only when q₀ is small.
A large q₀ would also feel a magnetic force, which would spoil the measurement.
questions.concept: Why the test charge in E = F/q0 must be vanishingly small
questions.why: A finite test charge exerts its own forces back on the source charges, displacing them and altering the very field being measured, so the limit of small q0 is needed for E to be a property of the sources.

questions.q: A single point charge sits alone in otherwise empty space. Which statement is correct?
options: It feels a force from its own field, directed radially outward.
It produces no field, since a field requires two charges to exist.
It produces a field everywhere, but feels no net force from that field.
Its field exists only at points where another charge has been placed.
questions.concept: A charge produces a field everywhere but exerts no net force on itself
questions.why: The field is defined by the force it would exert on a second charge; a lone charge's own field is real everywhere but cannot produce a net self-force.

questions.q: Two electric field lines can never cross one another. The reason is that:
options: field lines are only ever drawn emerging from positive charges.
a crossing point would have to be a point of zero field strength.
field lines repel each other in the way that like charges do.
the field at a point has one direction, and a crossing would give it two.
questions.concept: Why field lines never cross
questions.why: The field at any point has a single, unique direction - the tangent to the line there - and a crossing would assign two directions to one point, meaning two different forces on the same test charge.

questions.q: Why may the potentials due to several charges be added as ordinary signed numbers, while the fields must be added as vectors?
options: Potential is energy per unit charge, and energy has no direction — only a sign.
Potential is always a positive quantity, so no conflict of signs can arise.
Potential falls off as 1/r rather than 1/r², so the directions cancel out.
Potential is defined only along a field line, which already fixes its direction.
questions.concept: Why potentials add algebraically while fields add vectorially
questions.why: Potential is energy per unit charge and energy is a scalar, so each contribution carries only a sign, not a direction - there is nothing to resolve into components.

questions.q: At the exact midpoint between two equal positive charges, **E** = 0 but V ≠ 0. Which account of this is right?
options: V must be zero there too, since V is obtained directly from E by division.
E vanishes because the two charges are equal; V survives because it depends on their sign.
The field contributions are opposite arrows that cancel; the potentials are positive numbers that add.
E vanishes because the midpoint is where both field lines terminate; V survives because work was done reaching it.
questions.concept: Zero field with non-zero potential at the midpoint of two like charges
questions.why: The two field contributions are equal-magnitude arrows pointing opposite ways and cancel, while the two potential contributions are both positive numbers and simply add.

questions.q: A charged particle moves through a region containing both an electric and a magnetic field. Which statement about the Lorentz force is correct?
options: The magnetic term does work on the particle and so changes its speed.
The magnetic term stays perpendicular to **v**, so it turns the particle but cannot speed it up.
The magnetic term acts on the charge whether or not the particle happens to be moving.
The electric term acts only while the particle is in motion.
questions.concept: Structure of the Lorentz force: the magnetic term does no work
questions.why: The q(v x B) term is always perpendicular to v, so it supplies turning but zero power, changing direction while leaving speed and kinetic energy unchanged.

questions.q: Which of the following is a true statement about Coulomb's law as it was given this week?
options: It applies to any two charged objects, whatever their size or separation.
The distance r is measured between the nearest surfaces of the two bodies.
Doubling both charges and also doubling the separation halves the force.
It is stated for point charges at rest, spheres being treated from their centres.
questions.concept: Domain of validity of Coulomb's law
questions.why: The law as stated holds for point charges at rest, with uniformly charged spheres treated as points at their centres; r is centre-to-centre, not surface-to-surface.

questions.q: Coulomb's law is a statement about exactly two charges. Explain why the superposition principle is what licenses you to use it on a system of five charges, and say what would have to be true of nature for that step to fail.
questions.concept: Superposition is what licenses extending a two-body law to many bodies
questions.why: Coulomb's law tells you the force between exactly two charges and nothing more. Superposition is the separate, experimentally established claim that the force between any two charges is completely unaffected by the presence of others, so the total force on one charge is the vector sum of the pairwise Coulomb forces from each of the other four taken one at a time. Without it there is no route from a two-charge law to a five-charge system. It would fail if nature were non-linear in this respect - if a third charge could screen, enhance or otherwise modify the q1-q2 interaction, so that a pairwise force depended on what else was in the room.

questions.q: The electric field at a point is said to be a property of the source charges alone, even though it is *defined* by putting a test charge there and measuring a force. Explain why this is not a contradiction.
questions.concept: Definition by measurement versus ownership of the quantity
questions.why: The test charge is a probe, not a participant: it is used to reveal the field and is required to be vanishingly small precisely so that it does not disturb the sources. Dividing the measured force by q0 removes every trace of the probe from the result, and the ratio F/q0 comes out the same whatever test charge was used. So although a test charge appears in the definition, it appears only in order to be cancelled out. The field is therefore fixed entirely by the source charges and their positions, and exists at points where no test charge has ever been placed.

questions.q: Halfway between two equal positive charges the field is zero, but halfway between a positive and an equal negative charge it is not. Explain why, in terms of the directions of the two contributions — and say what happens to the *potential* in each of those two cases.
questions.concept: Directions decide cancellation for E, signs decide it for V - and they differ
questions.why: Between two equal positive charges each field contribution points away from its own charge, so at the midpoint the two arrows point in opposite directions and, being equal in magnitude, cancel to zero. Between a positive and an equal negative charge the field of the positive points away from it while the field of the negative points toward it - both in the same direction - so at the midpoint they reinforce and the field is at its largest. The potentials behave oppositely, because they carry a sign rather than a direction: two positive charges give two positive contributions that add to a non-zero maximum, while a positive and an equal negative give +kq/r and -kq/r, which sum to exactly zero. E and V therefore vanish in opposite configurations.

questions.q: Explain why a magnetic field can change the direction of a moving charged particle but never its kinetic energy, whereas an electric field can change both. Refer to the structure of the Lorentz force in your answer.
questions.concept: The magnetic term of the Lorentz force is always perpendicular to the velocity
questions.why: The Lorentz force is F = qE + q(v x B). The magnetic term is a cross product with v, so it is perpendicular to v at every instant. Work is force times displacement along the direction of motion, and a force always perpendicular to the motion has no component along it, so the magnetic term does zero work and the kinetic energy cannot change - it can only turn the particle, which is why charged particles follow circular or helical paths in a uniform magnetic field. The electric term qE carries no such constraint: its direction is fixed by E independently of v, so it generally has a component along the motion, does work, and changes both speed and direction.

checks.topic: The Wednesday deep hour takes Week 2's material conceptually, without traces or arithmetic. It starts from the lesson's own definition of a problem-solving strategy - a plan, made of multiple steps, used to find a solution or overcome a challenge - and the claim that different problems require different strategies, so that choosing and then studying a strategy's rules and procedures is part of solving rather than a delay. It then works through the internal mechanism of each of the six named strategies: brainstorming's dependence on volume of ideas and on deferred criticism; the heuristic trade of rationality for speed, valid only where a sub-optimal solution is acceptable; trial-and-error's cost scaling with the number of candidate solutions; means-ends analysis fixing the intended solution in advance and decomposing the problem so each part gets its best-suited approach; abstraction deleting the attributes that will not help reach a solution and leaving a model; and analogy transferring understanding from a known system, valid only while the underlying principles are the same. For each, the session asks what it costs and under what conditions it fails. The second half covers the conceptual basis of the week's classifications: well-defined versus ill-defined, and routine versus non-routine as a question of whether a standard method exists rather than whether arithmetic is involved. It closes on solvability - what the universal Turing machine contributes to the idea of an algorithm, and why "unsolvable" is a claim about the absence of a systematic decision procedure for every input rather than a claim that no answer exists, with decidable and undecidable problems and the halting problem treated in those terms.

questions.q: Trial-and-error is described as time-consuming and inefficient in some cases but perfectly reasonable in others. What decides which?
options: Whether the problem is well-defined or ill-defined
How many candidate solutions have to be tried before one works
Whether the solver has met a similar problem before
Whether the answer eventually reached is optimal or merely acceptable
questions.concept: Trial-and-error's cost is driven by the size of the candidate set, not by difficulty
questions.why: The lesson ties its efficiency solely to whether the number of possible solutions is few; many candidates make it time-consuming and inefficient.

questions.q: Heuristics let a decision be made "without stopping to think about the next course of action." In the lesson's terms, what is surrendered in exchange for that speed?
options: The requirement that the problem first be broken down into smaller sub-problems
The possibility of applying the strategy jointly with a group of colleagues
The need for the required facts and numbers to be supplied with the problem
The guarantee that the result is rational, so only sub-optimal outcomes are safe
questions.concept: The heuristic trade-off: speed and energy saved against rationality of the result
questions.why: Heuristics solve fast but their solutions are not always rational, so they are only appropriate where a sub-optimal solution is acceptable.

questions.q: What exactly does abstraction do to a problem, and what is the thing it leaves behind called?
options: Deletes the attributes that will not help reach a solution, leaving a model
Deletes the hardest parts of the problem so that the remaining easy part can be solved
Restates the problem in fewer words so that it is easier to memorise and communicate
Splits the problem into smaller sub-problems, each of which is then solved separately
questions.concept: Abstraction as deletion of non-contributing attributes, producing a model
questions.why: Abstraction filters out unneeded attributes and removes the patterns that will not help reach a solution; the essential idea left behind is called a model.

questions.q: Why does means-ends analysis reduce the work of a large problem in a way that simply attacking it head-on does not?
options: It replaces the original problem with a smaller one whose answer is close enough to serve
It generates a large number of candidate ideas at once, so a workable one is likely to appear
It settles the intended solution in advance, then splits the problem and gives each part its best-suited approach
It strips out every part of the problem that does not contribute directly to reaching the goal
questions.concept: Means-ends analysis as forward planning plus decomposition into best-suited sub-solutions
questions.why: It settles the intended solution beforehand, breaks the problem into smaller problems, and solves each with the best possible approach until the main problem is solved.

questions.q: Brainstorming forbids criticism of ideas while the session runs. What is the mechanism-level reason?
options: Criticism is unprofessional and damages the morale of the team taking part
Every idea offered in a brainstorming session is equally likely to be the correct one
The group is required to reach full consensus before any single idea may be judged
The method runs on volume of ideas and on fine-tuning others' ideas; criticism kills both
questions.concept: Why brainstorming defers criticism - the method runs on idea volume and on refining others' ideas
questions.why: Its two rules are to avoid criticism and to gather as many ideas as possible, and it works by fine-tuning other people's ideas; criticism suppresses both mechanisms.

questions.q: An analogy transfers understanding from a system you already know to a new one. Under what condition does that transfer remain valid?
options: The two systems belong to the same industry or field of study
The underlying principles of the two systems are the same
The earlier system's solution was the optimal one available
Both systems are well-defined, with clear goals and solution paths
questions.concept: The validity condition on analogical transfer
questions.why: Analogy uses existing understanding of a similar system only as long as the underlying principles are the same - a shared field of study or an optimal earlier solution is irrelevant.

questions.q: What makes a problem non-routine?
options: No standard method for solving it exists, so a novel method must be developed
Its solution cannot be reached by arithmetic operations, however involved
It has no single correct answer, only a range of acceptable approximations
It takes a long time to solve, even in the hands of an experienced solver
questions.concept: Non-routine defined by absence of a standard method, not by absence of arithmetic
questions.why: A non-routine problem is one for which no standard method of solving exists, so a novel method must be developed by the solver.

questions.q: In this lesson, calling a problem "unsolvable" is a claim about what?
options: The answer: no answer to the problem exists at all
The machine: the UTM's tape is finite, so it runs out of space
The method: no systematic method exists for deciding it, for every input value
The time: it runs longer than any computer could, though a faster machine would help
questions.concept: 'Unsolvable' as a claim about decision procedures, not about the existence of answers
questions.why: The lesson states explicitly that unsolvable problems are not ones for which no solution can be found; there is no systematic method for deciding them for every input, hence 'unsolvable decision problems'.

questions.q: The lesson says that after choosing a strategy, "the rules and procedures of that strategy must be studied." Explain why choosing and studying a strategy first is treated as part of solving the problem, rather than as a delay before solving it.
questions.concept: Choosing and studying a strategy is part of the solving, not a preliminary to it
questions.why: The lesson's claim is that different problems require different strategies, so the choice of strategy determines what you actually do to the problem - and therefore determines the outcome, not merely the speed of reaching it. A strategy applied without knowing its rules and procedures is applied wrongly: a heuristic used where an exact answer is required, or a brainstorming session run with criticism allowed, produces a bad result rather than a slow one. Studying the strategy is what makes the subsequent steps correct, so it is doing the work rather than delaying it.

questions.q: Explain why the halting problem is called *undecidable* rather than merely *very difficult* — and why undecidable problems are described as a subset of unsolvable ones.
questions.concept: Undecidable means no algorithm exists, not that none has yet been found
questions.why: Difficulty is a statement about cost - a very difficult problem still has a method, and a faster machine or a cleverer programmer improves matters. Undecidability is a statement about existence: it has been proved that no algorithm whatsoever can return a correct true/false answer for every possible input, so no amount of time, memory or ingenuity will produce one. The halting problem is of this kind. Undecidable problems are a subset of unsolvable ones because 'unsolvable' in this lesson means there is no systematic method for deciding the problem for every input, and undecidable problems are exactly the decision problems for which that has been proved.

questions.q: Abstraction and means-ends analysis both leave you with something smaller than the original problem. Explain why they are nevertheless different operations, and what each one does to the information in the problem.
questions.concept: Abstraction discards information; means-ends analysis preserves it and partitions it
questions.why: Abstraction removes attributes: it deletes the features of the problem that will not help reach a solution, and what remains is a model - smaller because information has been thrown away, and a genuine simplification of the original. Means-ends analysis removes nothing: it fixes the intended solution in advance and then divides the whole problem into smaller problems, each solved by its best-suited approach, so all the information is still present, merely distributed across the parts. One produces a single simpler problem; the other produces several complete smaller ones.

questions.q: Explain why a heuristic is a sound choice for picking a brand of rice in a shop but an unsound one for deciding how much money Dan gave away, given the two things a heuristic trades against each other.
questions.concept: A heuristic trades rationality of outcome against speed of decision
questions.why: A heuristic buys a fast decision at the cost of any guarantee that the result is rational or optimal, so it is sound exactly where a sub-optimal answer is acceptable. Choosing a brand of rice is such a case: the cost of a slightly worse choice is trivial, and the time saved by not comparing every brand is worth more than the accuracy given up. How much money Dan gave away is not: an exact algorithm exists, the question demands the exact figure, and 'about 200' is simply wrong. The trade is only worth making when the loss on the accuracy side is one you can afford.

checks.topic: This session works the same Week 2 function material as problems: reading a question, choosing a method, executing it accurately and checking the result. It covers evaluating compositions in the correct order and seeing that f o g and g o f differ; finding the largest domain of an expression that combines a logarithm with a denominator, where two separate restrictions must both be imposed; completing the square on a quadratic to locate its vertex, axis of symmetry and direction of opening; solving an absolute-value equation by splitting it into its two cases; solving an exponential equation by isolating the power and recognising it as a power of the base; evaluating a piecewise function at and either side of its boundary point by first deciding which condition the input satisfies; recovering a line's equation from two points via the slope formula and point-slope form; and solving a logarithmic equation by combining logs, clearing the log, and then rejecting the root that violates the domain. The written questions are diagnostic: naming exactly where standard wrong routes go astray - squaring an absolute-value equation and manufacturing extraneous roots, treating 5^x as 5 times x, taking c to be the vertex y-coordinate - and checking a vertex by independent means before reading end behaviour off a cubic.

questions.q: With f(x) = 2x + 3 and g(x) = x² − 1, the value of (f ∘ g)(2) is
questions.concept: Order of composition
questions.why: (f o g)(2) means f(g(2)): g(2) = 3, then f(3) = 2(3) + 3 = 9; option a) is g o f, b) multiplies the values, d) composes in the wrong place.

questions.q: The largest set of real x for which f(x) = log₁₀(x − 2) + 1/(x − 5) is defined is
options: x > 2 with x ≠ 5
x ≥ 2 with x ≠ 5
all real x except x = 5
questions.concept: Combining two separate domain restrictions
questions.why: log(x - 2) needs x - 2 > 0 strictly, and 1/(x - 5) needs x != 5, so both conditions apply simultaneously.

questions.q: The vertex of f(x) = 2x² − 12x + 7 is at
questions.concept: Completing the square to find a vertex
questions.why: 2x^2 - 12x + 7 = 2(x - 3)^2 - 11, so the vertex is (3, -11); option b) is the slide's error of taking c as the vertex height.

questions.q: The solution set of |2x − 5| = 7 is
options: x = 6 only
x = 6 or x = −1
x = 6 or x = 1
x = 1 or x = −6
questions.concept: Two-case method for absolute-value equations
questions.why: 2x - 5 = 7 gives x = 6 and 2x - 5 = -7 gives x = -1; both branches must be taken.

questions.q: Solving 3·2^x = 96 gives x =
options: log₂96 ≈ 6.6
questions.concept: Isolating the power before solving
questions.why: Divide first: 2^x = 32 = 2^5, so x = 5; option b) comes from reading 2^x as 2x and c) from stopping at 32.

questions.q: For f(x) = 3x + 4 when x ≤ 1 and f(x) = x² when x > 1, the value of f(1) + f(3) is
questions.concept: Selecting the correct piecewise branch
questions.why: x = 1 satisfies x <= 1 so f(1) = 7, and x = 3 satisfies x > 1 so f(3) = 9, giving 16.

questions.q: The line through (−2, 5) and (4, −7) has equation
options: y = −½x + 4
questions.concept: Line through two points
questions.why: m = (-7 - 5)/(4 + 2) = -2, and y - 5 = -2(x + 2) gives y = -2x + 1; d) uses x = +2 when finding the intercept.

questions.q: The solution of log₁₀x + log₁₀(x − 3) = 1 is
options: x = 10 or x = 13
x = 5 or x = −2
questions.concept: Domain check after solving a logarithmic equation
questions.why: Combining gives x^2 - 3x - 10 = 0 with roots 5 and -2, but x = -2 makes log x undefined, so only x = 5 survives.

questions.q: The equation |x − 4| = −3 has no solution, yet a student who squares both sides obtains x = 1 and x = 7. Say why there is no solution, and say precisely what the squaring step did to produce those two values.
questions.concept: Squaring is not a reversible step: it manufactures extraneous roots
questions.why: |x - 4| is an absolute value, so it is non-negative for every real x, while the right-hand side is -3; a non-negative quantity can never equal a negative one, so the equation has no solution and no algebra can produce one. Squaring both sides gives (x - 4)^2 = 9, which discards the sign information entirely, because the square of -3 and the square of +3 are the same number - so the squared equation is really solving |x - 4| = +3. Its roots x = 1 and x = 7 are the solutions of that different equation, and both fail when substituted back into the original. That is exactly why every root obtained after squaring must be checked in the original equation.

questions.q: You have found the vertex of f(x) = 2x² − 12x + 7 to be (3, −11). Give two independent checks — not a repeat of the completing-the-square work — that confirm this is right.
questions.concept: Independent checks on a computed vertex
questions.why: Check one, the axis of symmetry: the vertex's x-coordinate must equal -b/(2a) = 12/4 = 3, which matches, and this uses a formula rather than a repeat of the completing-the-square algebra. Check two, symmetry of the function values: points equidistant either side of x = 3 must have equal f-values, and f(2) = 8 - 24 + 7 = -9 while f(4) = 32 - 48 + 7 = -9, confirming symmetry about x = 3, with f(3) = 18 - 36 + 7 = -11 confirming the height. Since a = 2 > 0 the parabola opens upward, so -11 must be a minimum, and both neighbouring values being larger confirms that too.

questions.q: A student solves 5^x = 40 by writing x = 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Explain what that student has misread about the expression 5^x, and give the correct one-line method together with roughly what x is.
questions.concept: An exponent is not a multiplier
questions.why: The student has read 5^x as 5 times x, and has therefore solved 5x = 40. In 5^x the x is the exponent - the number of times 5 is used as a factor - not a coefficient, so the operation that undoes it is a logarithm, not division. The correct one-line method is x = log base 5 of 40, that is log 40 / log 5. Since 5^2 = 25 and 5^3 = 125, x lies between 2 and 3, and is roughly 2.3.

questions.q: For f(x) = −x³ + 3x² − 2, state the degree and leading coefficient, then say what f(x) does as x → +∞ and as x → −∞. Show the reasoning that gets you there, not just the conclusion.
questions.concept: End behaviour read off the degree and leading coefficient
questions.why: f(x) = -x^3 + 3x^2 - 2 has degree 3 and leading coefficient -1. For large |x| the term -x^3 dominates, because dividing either lower-degree term by -x^3 gives 3x^2/(-x^3) = -3/x and -2/(-x^3) = 2/x^3, both of which tend to 0 - so the lower terms become negligible relative to the leading term, not zero in themselves. As x tends to +infinity, x^3 tends to +infinity so -x^3 tends to -infinity, hence f(x) tends to -infinity. As x tends to -infinity, x^3 tends to -infinity so -x^3 tends to +infinity, hence f(x) tends to +infinity. This is the standard odd-degree, negative-leading-coefficient shape: up on the left, down on the right.

checks.topic: The Friday deep hour works the same week-2 material as problems. It concentrates on setting up superposition calculations from a free-body sketch: identifying each pairwise force, deciding from the signs whether it is an attraction or a repulsion, and therefore whether contributions add or subtract along the line - the single step where most marks are lost. It carries the arithmetic through with unit conversions (nm, um, nC, uC) intact and with the Coulomb constant applied correctly. The session works the three problems set in the deck: the electron on the line between two protons 3.6 nm apart, the three collinear charges of -18 uC, -12 uC and +24 uC and the net force on each, and the +2.00 nC / -5.00 nC pair whose resultant field at an intermediate point must be found and then converted to a force on an electron placed there. It also drills route selection - recognising when symmetry gives an answer instantly versus when a brute-force component sum is unavoidable - and error diagnosis, such as spotting that a net force larger than either contributing force means opposing contributions were wrongly added. Finally it covers checking a finished answer, either by dimensional analysis or by recomputing through a second independent relation. The emphasis throughout is on the set-up and the check, not on recalling statements.

questions.q: Two protons sit 3.6 nm apart, with an electron on the line between them, 1.2 nm from one proton. Which expression gives the magnitude of the net force on the electron?
questions.concept: Setting up collinear superposition when the two forces oppose
questions.why: The electron is attracted to both protons, which lie on opposite sides of it, so the contributions subtract; the relevant distances are 1.2 nm and 3.6 - 1.2 = 2.4 nm.

questions.q: Evaluate that net force (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², e = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C).
questions.concept: Executing that calculation with correct nm-to-m conversion
questions.why: ke^2 = 2.301x10^-28; dividing by 1.44x10^-18 and by 5.76x10^-18 gives 1.598x10^-10 and 3.996x10^-11 N, whose difference is 1.2x10^-10 N.

questions.q: Q₁ = −18 µC sits at x = −9 m, Q₂ = −12 µC at x = +1 m, and Q₃ = +24 µC at x = +7 m. The net electric force on Q₁ is:
options: 4.2 × 10⁻³ N toward −x
4.2 × 10⁻³ N toward +x
3.5 × 10⁻² N toward −x
1.5 × 10⁻² N toward +x
questions.concept: Net force on an end charge with one repulsion and one attraction
questions.why: F12 = 1.942x10^-2 N pushes Q1 along -x (both charges negative) while F13 = 1.517x10^-2 N pulls it along +x, leaving 4.2x10^-3 N toward -x.

questions.q: For the same three charges, the net electric force on Q₂ is:
options: 5.3 × 10⁻² N toward +x
9.1 × 10⁻² N toward +x
9.1 × 10⁻² N toward −x
7.2 × 10⁻² N toward +x
questions.concept: Recognising when two pairwise forces reinforce rather than oppose
questions.why: On Q2 the repulsion from Q1 (1.942x10^-2 N) and the attraction toward Q3 (7.192x10^-2 N) both point along +x, so they add to 9.1x10^-2 N toward +x.

questions.q: A +2.00 nC charge is at the origin and a −5.00 nC charge is at x = 0.800 m. The electric field at x = 0.200 m is:
options: 325 N/C in the +x direction
574 N/C in the −x direction
449 N/C in the +x direction
574 N/C in the +x direction
questions.concept: Field superposition between an unlike pair, where the contributions reinforce
questions.why: E1 = 449.5 N/C points away from the +2.00 nC charge and E2 = 124.9 N/C points toward the -5.00 nC charge; both lie along +x, giving 574 N/C in the +x direction.

questions.q: An electron is now placed at x = 0.200 m in that same field. The force on it is:
options: 9.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N in the −x direction
9.2 × 10⁻¹⁷ N in the +x direction
5.7 × 10² N in the −x direction
1.8 × 10⁻¹⁶ N in the −x direction
questions.concept: Converting a field to a force on a negative charge
questions.why: F = |q|E = (1.60x10^-19)(574.4) = 9.2x10^-17 N, and the electron's negative charge reverses the direction relative to E, giving -x.

questions.q: A student's algebra for the field of a point charge comes out as E = kq/r. A units check condemns it because:
options: kq/r carries units of N·C/m, which is not a unit of anything in this topic.
kq/r carries units of N·m/C, which is a volt — a potential, not a field.
kq/r carries units of N/C, so the units are fine and the mistake lies elsewhere.
kq/r carries units of J/C², which is neither a field nor a potential.
questions.concept: Using dimensional analysis to condemn a wrong expression
questions.why: kq/r has units (N.m^2/C^2)(C)/m = N.m/C = J/C = volt, which is a potential rather than the N/C a field requires - the error is one missing power of r.

questions.q: Four equal positive charges sit at the corners of a square and you must find **E** at its centre. The quickest correct route is to:
options: add the four magnitudes kq/r², since all four charges are equal and positive.
find the potential at the centre first, then divide it by the corner-to-centre distance.
note that the charges pair up across the diagonals, so the field is zero by symmetry.
sum the fields of two adjacent charges and double the result, by the square's symmetry.
questions.concept: Choosing a symmetry route over brute-force summation
questions.why: The four equidistant equal charges pair up across the diagonals into equal and opposite field vectors, so E at the centre is exactly zero without any arithmetic.

questions.q: You compute the net force on a charge that is being pulled in opposite directions by two others, and your answer comes out larger than either individual force. Explain what has almost certainly gone wrong, and how you would locate the error without redoing the whole calculation.
questions.concept: A net force larger than either contribution means opposing forces were added
questions.why: If two forces genuinely pull a charge in opposite directions, the resultant is their difference and must therefore be smaller than the larger of the two. A resultant larger than either one means the contributions were added when they should have been subtracted - that is, the direction of one force was assigned wrongly, almost always by misreading an attraction as a repulsion or by getting wrong which charge lies on which side. To locate it without redoing the arithmetic, sketch the charges on a line and mark the direction of each pairwise force from the signs alone: like repels, unlike attracts. Compare those arrows against the signs used in the sum, and the mismatched one is the error.

questions.q: Before doing any arithmetic, explain how you would decide whether the point of zero net field between two unequal *like* charges lies nearer the larger or the smaller charge — and why, for two charges of *opposite* sign, no such point exists between them at all.
questions.concept: Where a null point sits, and why it cannot lie between unlike charges
questions.why: The null point requires the two field magnitudes to be equal. The larger charge makes the stronger field at any given distance, so its contribution can only be matched by viewing it from further away - which places the null point nearer the smaller charge, and between the two when the charges are alike, since only there do the contributions oppose. For charges of opposite sign the picture changes: between them the field of the positive points away from it and the field of the negative points toward it, so both point the same way and reinforce everywhere along that segment. Since they never oppose there they can never cancel there, and the null point moves outside the pair, beyond the smaller charge.

questions.q: Explain why you should substitute charge *magnitudes* into F = k|q₁q₂|/r² and fix the direction from a sketch, instead of substituting the signed values and trusting the sign of the answer. Illustrate with the Q₁/Q₃ pair from question 3.
questions.concept: Magnitudes into the formula, directions from the sketch
questions.why: Substituting signed values makes the sign of the answer carry two different meanings at once - the signs of the charges and the direction along an axis - and the formula has no way of knowing how the charges are arranged in space, so the resulting sign tells you nothing reliable about direction. Substituting magnitudes gives an unambiguous size, and the sketch settles the direction from a rule that never fails: like charges repel, unlike attract. For the Q1/Q3 pair, k|q1q3|/r^2 = (8.99x10^9)(18x10^-6)(24x10^-6)/16^2 = 1.52x10^-2 N. Q1 is negative and Q3 positive, so they attract, and since Q3 lies to the right of Q1 the force on Q1 is toward +x. The sketch, not the algebra, produced that direction.

questions.q: Show how a units check would catch each of these two errors: writing F = kq₁q₂/r instead of /r², and writing E = Fq instead of F/q. State the units you get in each case and what quantity, if any, those units actually belong to.
questions.concept: Units as a check on a half-remembered formula
questions.why: F = kq1q2/r has units (N.m^2.C^-2)(C)(C)/m = N.m, which is a joule - an energy, not a force. The missing power of r has turned the expression into something with the dimensions of work, which condemns it immediately; the correct /r^2 gives (N.m^2.C^-2)(C^2)/m^2 = N. E = Fq has units (N)(C) = N.C, which belongs to no quantity in electrostatics at all; the correct F/q gives N.C^-1, the unit of electric field. In both cases the units fail before any number is substituted, so the error is caught for free.

checks.topic: The Saturday session is COS_102 applied, working the week's method through on concrete cases rather than restating it. The student is given stated problems and has to classify them by testing rather than by surface appearance - recognising that Bridget's 50-question exam-marks problem is non-routine despite using only arithmetic, that the parking-space area is routine because a known formula applies, and that "approximate the number of hairs on your head" is non-routine rather than unsolvable. Scenarios are then read and matched to the strategy actually in use, including cases designed to mislead: XYZ Corporation's $2bn turnover target decomposed into quarterly and regional targets is means-ends analysis, while the doctor converging several weaker rays on a deep tumour after recalling an army dividing to take a fortress is analogy, not means-ends, despite the division into smaller parts. The session runs the two ordered procedures of the week in sequence - the three analogy steps and the three steps for attacking a non-routine problem. It traces the substitution puzzle one replacement at a time, obtaining BOOOB from BOB via the rules OB->BOOB and BOB->O. Finally it diagnoses attempts that went wrong: a heuristic applied to a routine problem where an exact answer is required, a brainstorming session ruined by immediate criticism, and a premature conclusion that a substitution puzzle does not come out. The halting problem is met applied, as a request to write a program that decides termination for any input.

questions.q: "An exam has 50 questions. 4 marks are awarded per correct response and 2 marks deducted per wrong one. Bridget scored 165. How many correct responses did she give?" How should this be classified, and why?
options: Routine — it is settled entirely by arithmetic operations on the given numbers
Unsolvable — there are two unknowns and only one equation relating them
Non-routine — no standard method presents itself, so the solver must devise one
Undecidable — no algorithm returns a true/false answer for every such input
questions.concept: Classifying an arithmetic-looking problem that has no standard method
questions.why: The exam-marks problem gives no immediately clear procedure, so the solver must devise one - the definition of non-routine - even though the arithmetic itself is elementary.

questions.q: Starting from the string **BOB** and applying the rule "replace `OB` with `BOOB`" once, what do you get?
options: BOOB
BBOOB
BOOBB
BOOOB
questions.concept: Tracing one substitution step accurately, at the right position in the string
questions.why: BOB contains OB at positions 2-3; replacing that OB with BOOB leaves the leading B and yields BBOOB.

questions.q: XYZ Corporation wants $2 billion turnover this year. The board fixes the annual figure, splits it into quarterly targets, splits each quarter by sales region, and lets each region choose the tactic that suits its own market. Which strategy is this?
options: Means-ends analysis
Abstraction
Trial and error
Brainstorming
questions.concept: Recognising means-ends analysis in a decomposition scenario
questions.why: The goal is fixed in advance, then split into quarterly and regional sub-problems each solved by its best-suited approach - exactly means-ends analysis.

questions.q: A doctor must destroy a tumour deep inside a patient with a high-intensity ray without burning the healthy tissue the ray must pass through. She recalls an army that captured a fortress by dividing into small groups that converged from many roads, and fires several weaker rays from different directions at once. Which strategy is this?
options: Means-ends analysis, because the single strong ray was broken up into several smaller rays
Abstraction, because the surrounding healthy tissue was filtered out of the model she used
Brainstorming, because a number of possible routes to the tumour were considered together
Analogy, because a previously understood system with the same principle was reused
questions.concept: Distinguishing analogy from means-ends when the analogy itself involves division
questions.why: The solution is imported wholesale from a previously understood system - the army and the fortress - whose underlying principle matches; the division is a feature of the source system, not a decomposition of this problem.

questions.q: Dan had $500 and now has $287; a student is asked how much he gave away. The student does not subtract, but says "about 200 — that feels right." Which diagnosis is correct?
options: He used trial and error where the number of possible answers was far too large
He used a heuristic on a routine problem, where a sub-optimal answer is not acceptable
He treated a non-routine problem as routine by reaching for a standard algorithm
He skipped the brainstorming stage, so no alternative candidate answers were raised
questions.concept: Diagnosing a strategy applied outside its conditions of use
questions.why: Estimating instead of subtracting applies a heuristic to a routine problem that has an exact algorithm, and here a sub-optimal answer is not acceptable.

questions.q: Two problems: (i) "Calculate the area of a 150 m × 2000 m parking space." (ii) "Give an approximate number of hairs on your head." How are they classified?
options: (i) routine, since a known formula applies; (ii) non-routine
(i) routine, (ii) unsolvable, since nobody can count them
(i) non-routine, since it is geometry and not plain arithmetic; (ii) non-routine
Both routine, since both end in a number produced by arithmetic
questions.concept: Applying the routine/non-routine test without over-reaching to 'unsolvable'
questions.why: The area has a known formula so it is routine; the hair count has no standard method but is not undecidable - no decision procedure is at stake.

questions.q: A lecturer asks the class to write one program that reads any other program plus its input and prints whether that program will finish or run forever. What is the correct response?
options: It is possible, but only for programs short enough to be read through in reasonable time
It is possible on a UTM, whose tape is unbounded, but not on any real modern computer
It is possible, but so slow in practice that the answer arrives long after it is useful
It is impossible — this is the halting problem, undecidable for every input
questions.concept: Recognising the halting problem when it is posed as an engineering task
questions.why: No algorithm returns an accurate true/false answer for every input, so the program is impossible in principle; speed, program length and choice of machine are all irrelevant.

questions.q: A design team decides to solve a new problem by analogy. In what order must they carry out the steps?
options: Find similarities → define the problem → generate ideas from the description
Generate ideas → define the problem → select an analogy that fits those ideas
Define the problem and generate analogies → find similarities and select one → generate ideas
Select an analogy → define the problem in its terms → check the underlying principles match
questions.concept: Executing the analogy procedure in its stated order
questions.why: The lesson's steps run: define the problem and generate analogies, then find similarities and select one, then use the description and similarities to generate ideas.

questions.q: A classmate tries `OB`→`BOOB` once on **BOB**, does not reach **BOOOB**, and concludes the puzzle does not come out. Give a sequence of replacements that does reach **BOOOB**, and explain why his conclusion was premature.
questions.concept: Failing to reach a target in one step is not proof that no sequence exists
questions.why: A sequence that works is BOB -> (OB to BOOB) -> BBOOB -> (OB to BOOB on the trailing OB) -> BBOBOOB -> (BOB to O on the BOB at positions 2-4) -> BOOOB. His conclusion was premature because he tried a single application of a single rule and treated that one failure as covering every possibility. The puzzle has two rules that may be applied any number of times, in any order, and at any matching position in the string, so the search space is a tree of sequences rather than a list of single moves. Exhausting one branch says nothing about the others, and establishing that a target is unreachable requires an argument about all sequences, not one trial.

questions.q: Bridget's exam-marks problem is solved with nothing but addition, subtraction and multiplication, yet it is classified as non-routine while "what is 500 − 287?" is routine. Explain what the solver has to do in the first case that he does not have to do in the second.
questions.concept: Routine versus non-routine turns on whether a method presents itself
questions.why: For 500 - 287 the solver recognises the operation immediately: the problem states which quantities to combine and the standard subtraction algorithm applies directly, so no method has to be invented. Bridget's problem states no such operation. The solver must first introduce the unknowns, notice that correct and wrong responses together must total 50, express the score as 4c - 2(50 - c), and only then does an equation appear that can be solved routinely. That construction step - devising a representation and a method where none was given - is what makes it non-routine, and it is entirely independent of how elementary the arithmetic then turns out to be.

questions.q: At XYZ Corp's idea session on the falling product quality, the manager explains why each suggestion won't work as soon as it is offered, and the session ends with three surviving ideas. Explain why this session did not produce what brainstorming is designed to produce.
questions.concept: Criticism during the session destroys the two mechanisms brainstorming runs on
questions.why: Brainstorming is designed to produce a large volume of ideas, weak and half-formed ones included, on the expectation that participants will fine-tune and build on each other's contributions. Criticising each suggestion as it arrives defeats both mechanisms: people stop offering ideas they suspect are weak, so the volume collapses, and an idea shot down immediately is never available for anyone to improve or combine with another. Three surviving ideas is the symptom - the session produced a filtered shortlist, which is what the later evaluation stage is for, instead of the wide pool of raw material the session was supposed to generate. The judging was not wrong in itself, only done at the wrong time.

questions.q: Apply means-ends analysis to XYZ Corp's declining product quality: state the overall goal, name two sub-problems it breaks into, and explain why attacking the sub-problems separately is legitimate here rather than a way of dodging the real problem.
questions.concept: Means-ends analysis on a real goal, and when decomposition is legitimate
questions.why: The overall goal is fixed in advance: restore product quality to an agreed standard by a stated date. Two sub-problems it breaks into are, first, identifying where in the production line the defects are being introduced, by inspecting output at each stage; and second, establishing whether the cause is materials, machine condition or operator training, and correcting it. Each can be given the approach that suits it - sampling and measurement for the first, testing and comparison for the second. This is legitimate rather than evasive because the two sub-problems together account for the whole of the original goal and their solutions recombine into it: fixing the identified stage and its identified cause is what restoring quality consists of. It would be dodging only if a hard part were set aside and the easy parts solved on assumptions the hard part might later overturn.

recapCandidates.topic: Why the electric field can vanish where the potential does not, and the potential vanish where the field does not - the consequence of E being a vector and V a scalar.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: E and V are introduced together, both fall off with distance and both are computed from the same charges, so they get treated as two names for one thing - which makes it seem paradoxical that one can be zero exactly where the other is largest.
whyQuestions: What is the unit of E and what is the unit of V, and what does each unit tell you the quantity is per unit of?
Why does a field contribution need a direction while a potential contribution needs only a sign?
At the midpoint between two equal positive charges, what are the two field arrows doing, and what are the two potential numbers doing?
Now make one of those charges negative. Which of E and V is zero at the midpoint, and which is at a maximum?
Why can you not recover E at a point just by dividing V at that point by a distance?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It identifies E as force per unit charge (N/C, a vector) and V as energy per unit charge (J/C, a scalar), and grounds the whole difference in the fact that force has a direction and energy does not.
It therefore adds field contributions as arrows that can point against each other and cancel, and potential contributions as signed numbers that cancel only when the signs of the charges differ.
It draws the consequence: two like charges give E = 0 and V at a maximum at the midpoint, while two unlike charges of equal magnitude give V = 0 and E at a maximum there - so the two quantities vanish in opposite configurations, and neither can be obtained from the other by a simple division.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Two charges of +q sit a distance 2a apart; take the midpoint M. FIELD: the left charge pushes a positive test charge to the right with magnitude kq/a^2; the right charge pushes it to the left with the same magnitude kq/a^2. Equal arrows, opposite directions, so E = 0 at M. POTENTIAL: each contributes +kq/a, a positive number with no direction, so V = kq/a + kq/a = 2kq/a, which is a maximum, not zero. Now flip the right-hand charge to -q. FIELD: the +q pushes the test charge to the right with kq/a^2, and the -q pulls it to the right with kq/a^2 - both now point the same way, so E = 2kq/a^2, a maximum. POTENTIAL: +kq/a from one and -kq/a from the other, so V = 0. The two cases have swapped exactly. Note the final trap: at M in the second case V = 0 yet E is at its largest, which is why V cannot be divided by a distance to recover E - the correct relation is that E measures the rate at which V changes with position, and V can pass through zero while changing very fast indeed.

recapCandidates.topic: What 'unsolvable' and 'undecidable' actually claim - and why they are statements about methods, not about answers.
recapCandidates.whyMisunderstood: The everyday sense of 'unsolvable' is 'has no answer', so the lesson's technical sense gets read that way, and 'undecidable' then sounds like a stronger word for 'very hard'. Both readings are wrong, and the lecture slide warning against the first is easy to skim past.
whyQuestions: In this course, what exactly is being claimed when a problem is called unsolvable - about the answer, or about something else?
Does a program that is asked whether it halts have an answer at all, for a particular given input?
If every individual case has an answer, what is it that the halting problem says cannot be done?
Why does a faster computer, or more memory, not help with an undecidable problem, when it does help with a merely difficult one?
Why are undecidable problems described as a subset of unsolvable ones rather than as a separate category?
recapCandidates.goodAnswerContains:
It states the lesson's own correction explicitly: unsolvable problems are not problems for which no solution can be found - the claim is that no systematic method exists for deciding them for every input.
It separates the individual case from the general procedure: any particular program either halts on a given input or does not, so every instance has a true answer; what fails to exist is one algorithm that returns the right answer for all instances.
It distinguishes proved impossibility from cost, noting that difficulty is about time and resources - where a faster machine helps - while undecidability has been proved, so no machine, however fast, can do it; and it places undecidable problems inside the unsolvable ones as exactly those decision problems for which this has been established.
recapCandidates.workedExample: Ask for H(P, I): a program that reads any program P and input I and prints HALTS or LOOPS, correctly, every time. First note the answer exists case by case: the program 'while true do nothing' loops, and 'print 1 and stop' halts - each individual question has a definite true answer, so this is not a case of 'no answer exists'. Now suppose H existed. Build a new program D that takes a program P, runs H on the pair (P, P), and then does the opposite of what H says: if H reports HALTS, D enters an infinite loop; if H reports LOOPS, D stops immediately. Now run D on itself. If D halts, then H(D, D) must have reported HALTS - but D was built to loop in that case, so it does not halt. If D loops, then H reported LOOPS - but D was built to stop in that case, so it halts. Either way the assumption produces a contradiction, so no such H can exist. Note carefully what has been proved: not that some particular program's behaviour is unknowable, but that no single general method works for every input. That is the difference between undecidable and merely difficult, and it is why a faster machine changes nothing.
